analysis.one_liner:
Repeals the health law's employer and individual insurance mandates, lets the White House consolidate agencies, and cuts congressional pay 5%.

**What happened:** It never got a vote. The bill was referred to five different committees, sent to a health subcommittee, and died there with zero cosponsors.
analysis.headline: The sole-sponsored bill — with zero cosponsors — died in committee without a single vote; the health law mandates, the Medicare payment board, and members' pay all stayed as they were.
analysis.plain_summary: A Georgia Democrat introduced a bill that would repeal the health law's requirements that large employers offer coverage and that individuals buy it, and would abolish the board set up to rein in Medicare payment growth. It would also let the White House budget office consolidate federal agencies, require a vote of Congress before any agency signs a contract, grant, or loan guarantee over $100 million with one private company, bar EPA pollution-control grants to projects outside the U.S., cap federal civilian vehicle purchases, and cut members of Congress's pay by 5%. It was referred to five committees on the day it was introduced, never advanced, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employers with 50 or more workers would have avoided the health law's coverage mandate and its penalties and reporting requirements; doctors, hospitals, and other providers would have avoided the Independent Payment Advisory Board, a mechanism designed to force Medicare savings; people who would otherwise have owed the individual-mandate penalty would have kept that money; and the administration would have gained two-year authority to consolidate federal agencies. Members of Congress would have taken a 5% pay cut after the 2014 election.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large employers and health care providers

how_it_helps.text: It strikes the employer-mandate section (26 U.S.C. 4980H) and its reporting requirements from the tax code, ending the requirement that large employers offer health coverage or pay a penalty [S2] [S3].
It ends the individual mandate by providing that the tax-code section imposing it no longer applies after enactment [S2] [S3].
It repeals the Independent Payment Advisory Board, the ACA panel created to force Medicare payment reductions if spending grew too fast [S2] [S3].
It grants the OMB director two-year authority to submit agency reorganization plans, so long as the plan reduces the number of agencies and produces cost savings [S3].
It requires Congress to approve, by joint resolution, any contract, grant, or loan guarantee over $100 million to a private entity in a fiscal year [S2] [S3].
It cuts each member of Congress's basic pay by 5% after the November 2014 election, in place of any scheduled pay adjustment [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on people who would lose the employer-coverage guarantee: repealing the employer mandate means large employers are no longer required to offer coverage or face a penalty, and repealing the individual mandate shrinks the pool of insured customers, which tends to raise premiums for those who stay. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers would bear the risk of removing a cost-control mechanism with no replacement. Federal employees whose jobs consolidation plans targeted, and agencies whose large contracts would need a vote of Congress, would also bear costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers losing coverage guarantees, Medicare beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Repealing the employer and individual mandates together would remove the mechanisms the ACA used to expand coverage; without the mandates, fewer people would have coverage and premiums in the individual market would be expected to rise, since healthy and sick customers would no longer be pooled by requirement [S2] [S3].
Repealing the Independent Payment Advisory Board removes a backstop designed to hold Medicare spending down if it grows too fast, with no replacement mechanism in the bill [S2] [S3].

Giving the OMB director authority to consolidate agencies concentrates reorganization power in the executive branch, and the bill's own findings acknowledge consolidation could eliminate over 1,000 federal jobs [S3].

Requiring a vote of Congress for every contract, grant, or loan guarantee over $100 million to a private entity would insert a new legislative step into routine federal operations, which could delay them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes real taxpayer-facing measures (congressional pay cut, vehicle-purchase caps, a review of duplicative programs) with provisions whose main beneficiaries are large employers and health care providers. Repealing the coverage mandates and the Medicare cost-control board would shift risk and cost back onto workers, patients, and taxpayers without an offsetting protection, and the contracting-approval requirement risks slowing ordinary government business. The good-government gestures are modest next to the health provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees on the day of introduction, then to a health subcommittee, and never came out of committee before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Barrow introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to five committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Rules, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform — splitting it across jurisdictions [S5].
In early January 2013 it was referred twice more, to a Health subcommittee, and no committee ever reported it [S5].
No other member cosponsored it [S4], and no floor vote or committee vote ever occurred; the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, large employers kept facing the employer-coverage mandate rather than being released from it, and health providers remained subject to the Medicare cost-control board. The public kept existing coverage protections, while members of Congress also avoided the 5% pay cut. Taxpayers got none of the promised consolidation savings — but no one lost anything either, since nothing in the bill had taken effect.

for.name: Rep. John Barrow
for.role: U.S. Representative, Georgia's 12th district; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to five committees; did not advance it further before losing his seat at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; never scheduled a markup or reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2013, sent its health provisions to the Subcommittee on Health, and took no further action before the Congress expired.

against.name: House Democratic and Republican caucuses
against.role: All 434 other voting members of the House
against.what_they_did: No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The only partisan signal in the record is the sponsor himself — a single Democrat — with zero cosponsors from either party and no votes ever taken.

industries.note: Repealing the employer mandate frees them from penalties and reporting for not offering coverage; the cost is borne by workers who would lose the guarantee of an offer of coverage. The bill's own framework acknowledges workers would lose this requirement [S3].

industries.industry: Hospitals, doctors, and other Medicare providers
industries.note: Repealing the Independent Payment Advisory Board removes a mechanism designed to force Medicare payment reductions if spending grows too fast; providers' gain comes at the risk of faster Medicare cost growth for beneficiaries and taxpayers [S2] [S3].

Repealing the individual mandate shrinks their subsidized customer pool, but repealing the employer mandate and related reporting also lifts a mandate that steered customers to them and removes compliance obligations.
Large contracts, grants, and loan guarantees (over $100 million to a private entity) would need an act of Congress, adding delay and uncertainty to deals that today are signed by agencies [S3].

The bill's own findings project consolidation of commerce-related agencies would eliminate over 1,000 duplicative federal jobs, and OMB would gain standing authority to propose such consolidations [S3].

industries.industry: EPA grantees and foreign environmental programs
industries.note: Clean Air Act grant and contract money could no longer fund air-pollution control projects outside the United States [S2] [S3].
